steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our distributed computing paper on Process-Commutative Objects, a new class of distributed objects between BFT CRDTs and totally ordered ledgers. Motivate it from blockchains/cryptocurrencies and CRDTs, summarize our contributions, and give the paper outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Blockchains/DLT and BFT; total order and the cost of agreement
2. Cryptocurrencies don't need total order: practical and theoretical consequences
3. CRDTs: weak synchronization
4. BFT CRDTs and their limits (double spending)
5. This paper: Process-Commutative Objects, generic algorithm, examples
6. Paper outline

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. BFT and total order
- Blockchains / Distributed Ledger Technologies (DLT): renewed interest in Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT), field started more than 40 years ago (cite)
- BFT algorithms -> total order (TO) on operations despite malicious participants
- TO requires Byzantine-Tolerant Agreement; impossible deterministically in async systems (cite)
- so DLTs: high execution costs, compromise on termination or guarantees (cite)
  - probabilistic correctness (Bitcoin), or costly (randomized) synchronization (cite)

2. Cryptocurrencies without total order
- TO and Byzantine Agreement less central than first assumed
- recent works: cryptocurrency objects (first, most emblematic Blockchain application) don't need TO; FIFO reliable broadcast suffices (cite)
- practice: trustless money transfer much more efficient than full BFT TO implementations: Proof-of-Work (cite), BFT consensus (cite), Proof-of-Stake (cite)
- theory: characterize class of BFT objects implementable with plain FIFO reliable broadcast
- computational power of reliable (FIFO) broadcast matters: weaker than atomic registers

3. CRDTs
- weak synchronization for distributed objects not new
- Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) (cite): broad family of weakly synchronized distributed data structures
- no advanced synchronization; systematic reconciliation
- highly scalable, robust to transient disconnections and crashes; attractive for large-scale decentralized services

4. BFT CRDTs
- last few years: Byzantine-tolerant CRDT designs, CRDT strengths + BFT robustness (cite)
- CRDTs not designed to block conflicting updates -> can't prevent duplicitous actions of malicious participants that violate invariants when combined
- remediate by cancelling all/some incompatible operations when (eventually) detected
- cannot prevent double spending -> problem for cryptocurrencies

5. This paper
- territory between best-effort BFT CRDTs and totally ordered ledgers
- Mazurkiewicz traces -> Process-Commutative Objects (PCO)
- PCOs: Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC) + Pipeline Consistency (PC); conflicting operations allowed under conditions
- generic algorithm for any PCO specified by an appropriate trace language
- crash and Byzantine model, depending only on underlying reliable broadcast
- four examples: multisets, Petri Nets (building blocks); money transfer, work stealing deques (advanced)

6. Outline
- S2 background: Distributed Ledgers, CRDTs, BFT, BFT CRDTs
- S3 system model, trace monoid (algebraic structure)
- S4 formal spec of PCOs, crash-prone and Byzantine async
- S5, S6 generic algorithm + proofs
- S7 four examples: Multi-sets with Deletion Rights, Petri Nets with Transition Rights, Money Transfer, Work and Stealing Deques
- S8 conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Blockchains and Distributed Ledger Technologies (DLT) in general have brought new and growing interest to Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT), which is a field that started more than 40 years ago. Most modern Blockchains and DLTs use BFT algorithms to enforce a total order (TO) on their operations, even when there are malicious participants. The problem is that total ordering requires solving Byzantine-Tolerant Agreement, and this is a vexing problem that has been known for a long time to be impossible to solve deterministically in asynchronous systems.

Because of this, existing DLTs usually have high execution costs and have to make a compromise either on termination or on their guarantees, for example by only giving probabilistic correctness guarantees (Bitcoin), or by using costly (randomized) synchronization mechanisms.

However total ordering and Byzantine Agreement are less central to Blockchains and DLTs than people first assumed. Recent works showed that cryptocurrency objects, which are the first and maybe the most emblematic application of Blockchain, do not need a total order and can be implemented with weaker communication abstractions like FIFO reliable broadcast. This has far-reaching consequences, both in practice and in theory. In practice, it means that trustless money transfer applications can be implemented much more efficiently than the first implementations that were based on full BFT TO mechanisms (whether based on Proof-of-Work, BFT consensus, or Proof-of-Stake). In theory, it raises the question of characterizing the class of BFT distributed objects that can be implemented directly with a plain FIFO reliable broadcast. Delineating the computational power of reliable (FIFO) broadcast also has important ramifications, since reliable broadcast is weaker (computationally) than atomic registers.

Using weak synchronization for distributed objects is not new. It has been explored a lot for Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs), which are a broad family of weakly synchronized distributed data structures. CRDTs avoid the need for advanced synchronization by doing systematic reconciliation. Because of this pragmatic approach CRDTs are highly scalable, robust to transient disconnections and crashes, and especially attractive for implementing large-scale decentralized services.

In the last few years, several designs for Byzantine-tolerant CRDTs have been proposed that combine the strengths of traditional CRDTs with the robustness of BFT algorithms. But since CRDTs are not designed to block conflicting updates, these approaches cannot prevent duplicitous actions by malicious participants, which violate the invariant of an application when they are combined. Instead they usually remediate these attacks by canceling all or some of the incompatible operations when the problem is (eventually) detected. In particular, existing BFT CRDTs cannot prevent double spending, which is a problem for cryptocurrency applications.

This paper is a step to chart the territory between best-effort BFT CRDTs and totally ordered distributed ledgers. Using Mazurkiewicz traces, we introduce a new class of distributed objects that we call Process-Commutative Objects (PCO). PCOs give both Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC) and Pipeline Consistency (PC), and they allow conflicting operations under certain conditions. Then the paper proposes a generic algorithm that can implement any PCO that is specified by an appropriate trace language. The generic algorithm works in a crash model and in a Byzantine fault model, and which one depends only on the properties of the underlying reliable broadcast. Finally the paper gives four concrete examples of PCOs, from fundamental building blocks (multisets and Petri Nets) to more advanced mechanisms (money transfer objects and work stealing deques).

In Section 2 we give some background on Distributed Ledgers, CRDTs, Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT), and recent efforts to design BFT CRDTs. Section 3 defines our system model and presents the notion of trace monoid, the algebraic structure that the construction in this paper is based on. Section 4 formally specifies a new type of CRDTs that we call Process-Commutative Objects, both in crash-prone and in Byzantine asynchronous distributed systems. Based on these definitions, Sections 5 and 6 present and prove a generic algorithm that implements any Process-Commutative Object. Section 7 discusses four practical examples of Process-Commutative Objects that this algorithm can implement: (i) Multi-sets with Deletion Rights, (ii) Petri Nets with Transition Rights, (iii) Money Transfer, and (iv) Work and Stealing Deques. Section 8 concludes the paper.

BFT algorithms allow most modern Blockchains and DLTs to enforce a total order (TO) on their operations, even in the presence of malicious participants. Unfortunately, total ordering requires solving Byzantine-Tolerant Agreement, a vexing problem that has long been known to be impossible to solve deterministically in asynchronous systems [4].

As a result, existing DLTs typically have high execution costs and must strike a compromise regarding either termination or their guarantees [5] —for instance, by only providing probabilistic correctness guarantees (Bitcoin), or by using costly (randomized) synchronization mechanisms [6,7,8].

Total ordering and Byzantine Agreement are, however, less central to Blockchains and DLTs than first assumed. Recent works have shown that cryptocurrency objects, Blockchain's first and perhaps most emblematic application, do not require a total order and can be implemented using weaker communication abstractions, such as FIFO reliable broadcast [9,10,11]. This realization has far-reaching consequences, both practically and theoretically. In practice, it suggests that trustless money transfer applications can be implemented much more efficiently than initial implementations based on full-fledged BFT TO mechanisms (whether based on Proof-of-Work [12], BFT consensus [13,14], or Proof-of-Stake [15]). From a theoretical point of view, it raises the question of characterizing the class of BFT distributed objects that can be directly implemented using a plain FIFO reliable broadcast. Delineating the computational power of reliable (FIFO) broadcast in turn has important ramifications, as reliable broadcast is weaker (computationally) than atomic registers.

Using weak synchronization for distributed objects is not new. It has been extensively explored in the context of Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs for short) [16,17,18,19,20,21,22,23], a broad family of weakly synchronized distributed data structures. CRDTs avoid the need for advanced synchronization through systematic reconciliation. This pragmatic approach makes CRDTs highly scalable, robust to transient disconnections and crashes, and particularly attractive for implementing large-scale decentralized services.

Over the last few years, several designs for Byzantine-tolerant CRDTs have been proposed that combine the strengths of traditional CRDTs with the robustness of BFT algorithms [24,25,26,27]. Unfortunately, because CRDTs are not designed to block conflicting updates, these approaches cannot prevent duplicitous actions by malicious participants, which violate an application's invariant when combined. Instead, they typically remediate such attacks by canceling all or some of the incompatible operations when the problem is (eventually) detected. In particular, existing BFT CRDTs cannot prevent double spending, a problematic situation for cryptocurrency applications.

This paper is a step to chart the territory that lies between best-effort BFT CRDTs and totally ordered distributed ledgers. Using Mazurkiewicz traces, it introduces a novel class of distributed objects called Process-Commutative Objects (PCO for short). PCOs provide both Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC) and Pipeline Consistency (PC), while allowing conflicting operations under certain conditions. Finally the paper presents four concrete examples of PCOs, ranging from fundamental building blocks (multisets and Petri Nets) to more advanced mechanisms (money transfer objects and work stealing deques).

Section 2 first presents some background on Distributed Ledgers, CRDTs, Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT), and recent efforts to design BFT CRDTs. Section 3 then defines our system model and presents the notion of trace monoid, the algebraic structure that underpins the construction developed in this paper. Section 4 formally specifies a novel type of CRDTs that we call Process-Commutative Objects, both in crash-prone and in Byzantine asynchronous distributed systems. Building on these definitions, Sections 5 and 6 present and prove a generic algorithm that implements any Process-Commutative Object. Section 7 discusses four practical examples of Process-Commutative Objects that can be implemented by this algorithm: (i) Multi-sets with Deletion Rights, (ii) Petri Nets with Transition Rights, (iii) Money Transfer, and (iv) Work and Stealing Deques. Section 8 concludes the paper.
